a more in depth understanding of the ﬂuids which dominate the surface of our planet. We will begin the project with a quick review of the ﬂuid dynamics course covering the fundamental topics which the reader will be required to have an understanding of to fully engage with the topics dis- cussed later in the project. This prerequisite understanding will not only provide the reader with the governing equations of motion for ﬂuids but it will also attempt to give a full derivation of these equations. The reason we will take the time to derive these is due to the assumption that with the knowledge obtained from this analysis the reader will have a better understanding of the general topic which will result in more involved material for the reader overall. The prerequisite understanding section should also give the reader an indication of the type of analysis which will feature heavily throughout the project and help the reader to familiarise themselves with how the project will tackle derivation of equations throughout with derivations which are to a lower level of under- standing. Once we have completed the section on prerequisite understanding we will move on to our analysis of the motion of a ﬂuid in gravity waves. During this section, we will provide a full derivation of the paths of ﬂuid particle and velocity of wave propaga- tion in both deep and shallow water. The project will be using the equations of motion derived previously and applying these to sets of initial and boundary conditions to ob- tain the desired equations. Throughout the analysis of both deep and shallow water, we will provide a visual representation of the paths that the ﬂuid particle will take, this will provide the reader with a better understanding of how the ﬂuid will move in dif- ferent systems. The project will also show the reader how the ﬂuid particles motion can change with differing positions in both the x and z axes. During the discussion of wave propagation, there will be a small real world application which will provide an explanation to what we see on shores after a storm out at sea. Once we have derived the equations of motion for these gravity waves we will move our focus on to ﬂuids which posses note-able values of viscosity, ﬂuids such as glycer- ine for example. This analysis will show the reader how a change in the ﬂuid in which the waves are generated in can yield a substantial change in the overall motion of the waves. This section, as before, will provide the reader will visual representation of this damping effect in ﬂuids which will have a small and large dynamic viscosity, η. This visual representation is signiﬁcant because the equations alone do not show the extent that the viscosity inﬂuences the damping. Once the reader has a ﬁrm understanding of the gravity waves and damping the project will begin the analysis of capillary waves or ripples. During this ﬁnal section of mathe- matical analysis, we will develop our understanding of the smallest and most beautiful waves that we can ﬁnd in nature and how these waves can inﬂuence the larger waves which we have previously derived. We will begin with a discussion on the Laplace equa- tion which will develop the readers understanding of how we can derive equations that 4 will describe surface tension, the fundamental force for capillary waves which deﬁned there unique shape and hydrodynamic properties. During our derivation of the Laplace equation, we will use some simple geometry and well-known formulae found in physics to ﬁnd a relation between radii of curvature and displacement from the plane. Using the knowledge that the reader has developed from the Laplace equation the project will continue to derive the equations of motion governing capillary waves in a plane. The aim of this section is to show the reader how some basic characteristics can affect waves motion. Finally, this section will discuss how these special cases of waves are damped differently to that of a gravity wave using analysis techniques that the reader has de- veloped previously when discussing the damping of gravity waves. This will lead to a discussion of why the damping coefﬁcient is different for these types of waves. Finally, in the last section of the project, the reader will begin to develop an understand- ing of how imperfections in the conditions surrounding the ﬂuid can cause a difference in the characteristics of the wave. During the course of this section, the reader should expect less derivation of equations and more of a general discussion of how these exter- nal inﬂuences can affect the waves. The reason for this change is due to the difﬁculty in deriving equations for random events and we believe that the readers time will be better spent developing an understanding of why the wave characteristics differ instead of a mathematical derivation of how. The discussion will allow the reader to have a better understanding of the motion of waves in real world applications due to the real-world never having perfect conditions unless the system is produced in a laboratory. The reader will also begin to develop an understanding of what we as humans have been doing for centuries to manipulate the ﬂuid for our convenience. 1.2 Literature Review We will here provide the reader with a review of the literature that we have used throughout the project. These equations are crucial in the analysis of more complex ﬂuid motion that we will be studying throughout this project and evidently is important that we take the time to derive said equations. 2.1 Equation of continuity We begin our study of fundamental equations with the equation of continuity. This equation mathematically represents the condition that mass must be conserved in ﬂuid motion, it is a simple equation but one that is very important in any study of ﬂuids. If we consider a small volume, dV , which is enclosed by a surface, S, we know from a well know simple equation that the total mass of the ﬂuid is given by ∫ V ρ dV . We can also ﬁnd the value of total ﬂow out of a volume, V , by evaluating the total ﬂow through the surface S as these to statements are equivalent. We know that the total ﬂow through 6 a surface is given by ∮ S ρv · df . We can also ﬁnd the decrease in time of the mass of the ﬂuid in V to be − ∂ ∂t ∫ ρdV. By equating the two equations we ﬁnd ∂ ∂t ∫ ρdV = − ∮ S ρv · df . (1) Using Green’s formula which is deﬁned as ∮ S a · df = ∫ V ∇ · adV, (2) and applying this to (1) we arrive at ∫ V dV [∂ρ ∂t + ∇ · ρv] = 0. (3) As the volume is none zero we can simplify equation to the following ∂ρ ∂t + ∇ · ρv = 0, (4) which is the equation of continuity for a ﬂuid. It is important to note this is a general equation of continuity. During the course of this project, we will see two more instances where we encounter an equation of a different form that is still named the equation of continuity. This reoccurring naming of equations is not a mistake from the project the equation can simply take different forms for different systems, however, the function of the equation remains the same. 2.2 Euler’s equation The next equation of motion we will derive is Euler’s equation. Originally being pub- lished by Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler in his article named ”Principes g´en´eraux du mouvement des ﬂuides”, the equation provides us with a relation between velocity, density and pressure for ideal ﬂuids which express steady ﬂow. We begin by considering a volume, V , of a ﬂuid. We can express the total force acting on the volume to be − ∮ S pdf . 7 From the deﬁnition of force we have F = ∮ S df in our liquid. We also use the deﬁnition of pressure, dF = −pdf , which provides us with F = ∮ S dF = − ∮ p df . (5) If we now apply Green’s formula to the right hand side of equation (2) we ﬁnd F = ∮ S dF = − ∫ V ∇p dV. (6) If we consider an element of mass, m, we have ma = ∫ V a dm = ∫ V ρ dv dt dV. (7) If we now use, the well known, Newtons second law, F = ma and substitute equations (6) and (7) into the formula we arrive at ∫ V ρ dv dt dV = − ∫ V ∇p dV, which can be simpliﬁed to the following ρ dv dt = −∇p. (8) We know that dv dt is the rate of velocity for a moving ﬂuid particle and dv is an exact differential so by deﬁnition we have that dv dt = ∂v ∂t + dx dt ∂v ∂x + dy dt ∂v ∂y + dz dt ∂v ∂z . We also know from the deﬁnition of velocity that v = ( dx dt , dy dt , dz dt ) and from the deﬁni- tion of gradient we have ∇ = ∂ ∂x + ∂ ∂y + ∂ ∂z . If we apply these two deﬁnitions to our equation for acceleration we obtain dv dt = ∂v ∂t + (v · ∇)v, applying this to equation (8) we arrive at ∂v ∂t + (v · ∇)v = ∇p ρ (9) 8 this is Euler’s equation. However this is without the presence of gravity if we wanted it with gravity we simply need to add the term g which is Euler’s equation in the presence of gravity which can be seen below ∂v ∂t + (v · ∇)v = ∇p ρ + g. (10) 2.3 Bernoulli’s equation The ﬁnal equation of motion that we will cover in this section is Bernoulli’s equation. Bernoulli’s principle was originally published in Daniel Bernoulli’s book ”Hydrody- namica”, however, it was Euler who wrote the equation into the form that we know today as Bernoulli’s equation. This equation tells us how the speed of the ﬂuid relates to the pressure of the ﬂuid with density and gravity also considered. We begin our derivation of Bernoulli’s equation by using the deﬁnition of steady ﬂow which states ∂v ∂t = 0. This property is a result of the velocity not changing in time it can, however, change in space so for this system we have the following v(x, y, z, t) = v(x, y, z). We know from section 2.1 that Euler’s equation for a ﬂuid is deﬁned as ∂v ∂t + (v · ∇)v = ∇p + g If we consider an incompressible ﬂuid, ρ = constant, with a system that has an absence of gravitational ﬁeld, g = 0, and apply the deﬁnition (v · ∇)v = 1 2∇v2 − v × (∇ × v), proof of which can be found in the appendices, to Euler’s equation we obtain 1 2 ∇v2 − v × ∇ × v = −∇ ( p ρ ) . We now introduce the idea of a streamline. A streamline is a line who’s tangent gives the direction of the velocity at that moment. If we consider the above equation along a streamline and introduce a tangent unit vector ˆl. From the deﬁnition of a tangent we see that ˆl is parallel to v on a streamline, hence the element (v × ∇ × v) is perpendicular to ˆl. Therefore if we multiply the equation through by the dot product of ˆl we ﬁnd (∇(1 2 v2 + p ρ )) · ˆl = 0 on a streamline. We also have that the unit vector ˆl by deﬁnition is none zero hence we can simplify to ∇(1 2v2 + p ρ ) = 0. 9 As the gradient of 1 2v2 + p ρ is equal to zero we can then deduce that 1 2v2 + p ρ = C (11) where C is a constant. This is Bernoulli’s equation for an incompressible ﬂuid without the presence of gravity. In the case of gravity being present using similar procedures we get that Bernoulli’s equation in presence of gravity is 1 2 v2 + p ρ + gz = C (12) where C again is a constant. 2.4 Potential ﬂow Our ﬁnal section in the prerequisite understanding chapter is on potential ﬂow. Poten- tial ﬂow is not an equation that requires deriving it merely a deﬁnition of a ﬂuid when certain conditions are satisﬁed. For a ﬂow to be considered potential it must satisfy two conditions: the ﬂuid must be incompressible, ∇v = 0, and must have zero vorticity, ω = ∇×v = 0. From these def- initions, it follows that the velocity for a potential ﬂow can be written as v = ∇ϕ as we know that ∇×(∇ϕ) = 0. We can also take the divergence of v which gives us △ϕ = 0. By taking Euler’s equation (9) and make the substitution (v·∇)v = 1 2∇v2−v×(∇×v) as we did before in the section on Bernoulli’s equation, we arrive at the following ∂v ∂t + 1 2∇v2 − v × (∇ × v) = − 1 ρ ∇p. Using the deﬁnition of v = ∇ϕ for potential ﬂow and substituting this into the equation we obtain ∇(∂ϕ ∂t + 1 2 v2 + p ρ ) = 0, which ﬁnally simpliﬁes to ∂ϕ ∂t + 1 2 v2 + p ρ = f (t), (13) where f(t) is a function of time. We hope that content discussed in this section of the report will help the reader to now continue with the main body of text. 10 3 Gravity Waves 3.1 Introduction to Gravity Waves Gravity waves arise when some disturbance in the surface of the water causes a dis- ruption to the equilibrium of the water. In positions in which the water rises above the equilibrium, gravity will act upon the water and pull it down as the density of water is more than it is of the atmosphere. The inertia that is acquired from this falling motion reduces the water to below the equilibrium hence causing the water to again bob up above the equilibrium. This processes continues until the ﬂuid returns to equilibrium and displays an oscillating motion in the z-axis. The most obvious visualisation of this process is the waves found in the sea. We know that waves in the sea do not posses motion that is solely in the z-direction, however, they also propagate horizontally. To understand why this horizontal motion occurs, we consider an object that is dropped into the water that is at equilibrium, when the object enters the water the pressure sur- rounding the object is higher than that of the surrounding ﬂuid and because of this high relative pressure water accelerates away from the object in all directions causing a prop- agation of ﬂuid. It is important to note that these waves are still affecting the interior of the ﬂuid but at a lower amount the deeper that the ﬂuid is. 3.2 Linearisation We begin our analysis of gravity waves by considering how we can use the mathemat- ical process of linearisation to allow the method of deriving equations of motion to be much simpler for us. (17) 3.3 Deep Water Solution There are three different types of gravity waves which we will encounter in nature; deep water, shallow water and intermediate gravity waves. This project will consider the deep water and shallow water limits in this section. We will see that these limits will impact the shape of the ﬂuid particles path and the velocity of wave propagation. We will begin with the deep water solution. 3.3.1 Path of Fluid Particle The deep water limit states that λ << H where λ is the wavelength and H is the depth of the water. At this limit, we can neglect the boundary conditions at the bottom and the sides of the ﬂuid as the external waves produced will have decayed before it reaches the bottom surface. For our wave, we are making the assumption that we have the ﬂuid propagating along the x-axis and is uniform in the y-direction as ﬁgure one shows, with these assumptions we ﬁnd that our solution will be independent of the y-component. It is reasonable to assume that our solution for velocity potential will be in the form of a simple period function of time and the x coordinate hence we have the following equation for the potential φ = f (z)cos(kx − ωt) where ω is the angular frequency of the wave and k is the wave number which is equiv- alent to 2π λ . Recalling the deﬁnition △ϕ = 0 and substituting our value for the potential into said deﬁnition we ﬁnd ∂2f (z)cos(kx − ωt) ∂z2 − k2f (z)cos(kx − ωt) = 0. Clearly, we begin our analysis by ﬁnding a solution for f (z). To ﬁnd a solution for this function we ﬁx a value of time such that cos(kx − ωt) ̸= 0 which allows us to divide 14 the equation through by cos(kx − ωt). Doing this leaves us with the following relation for f (z) ∂2f (z) ∂z2 − k2f (z) = 0. The solution to this relation is given by f (z) = c1e kz + c2e −kz. From the deep water limit, we know that at the bottom surface of the ﬂuid we would observe no movement of ﬂuid. This limit allows us to deﬁne the boundary condition at the bottom surface given by z → −∞ f (z) = 0. If we apply this boundary condition to our solution for f (z) we ﬁnd c1e kz|z→−∞ + c2e−kz|z→−∞ = 0 it is clear that the ﬁrst term will decay away to 0 as → −∞ as it will become a power of a negative inﬁnity, however, for the second term it is clear that e−kz approaches inﬁnity for the limit. Therefore the second term does not satisfy our boundary condition except for c2 = 0 and we are left with the following solution for the velocity potential φ = c1ekzcos(kx − ωt). Damping of ﬂuid arises when there exists some internal friction between ﬂuid particles. This in- ternal friction results in the loss of kinetic energy in the system which yields the visual result of a wave’s amplitude becoming smaller in time. By the end of this section, we hope the reader will have obtained an understanding of how we can calculate the value for the damping coefﬁcient and how this coefﬁcient impacts the shape of ﬂuid motion in different ﬂuids. 4.1 Oscillations in a Viscous Fluid Before we can consider how damping effects gravity waves we must ﬁrst develop an understanding of how oscillations in a viscous ﬂuid behave. Let us begin by again considering oscillations at the surface of a ﬂuid, like the grav- ity waves we were studying in the previous section. We assume a body of ﬂuid that is incompressible and bounded by an inﬁnite plane surface which performs simple har- monic oscillations with frequency ω. We take the yz-plane to be the solid surface and the ﬂuid region to be x > 0 and take the y-direction to be the direction of oscillations. The velocity of these oscillations in this instance will be given by u whose solutions will be given in the form u = u0e−iωt where u0 is a constant given by Aeiα. If we only consider linear operations upon the velocity, u, we can assume that the solutions will only take the real part so we can continue using the complex solution of the velocity but at the ﬁnal solution we will consider only the real part, hence we have that uy = u = u0e −iωt. We also have that the ﬂuid must satisfy the boundary condition at x = 0 given by v = u, hence at x = 0 we have that ux = uz = 0, uy = u. It is clear that the oscillation is only dependant on x and time, t, so from the equation of continuity for incompressible ﬂuids, ∇v = 0 , we have ∂vx ∂x = constant = 0, from the boundary condition. As we have found that all terms are independent of y and z and vx does not depend on x it follows that the advection term, (v · ∇)v, is also zero. From this the Navier-Stokes equation becomes ∂v ∂t = − 1 ρ ∇p + ν△v (44) which is a linear equation whose x-component is ∂p ∂x = 0 or p = constant. It is clear that the y-component becomes vy = v, this leaves us with ∂v ∂t = ν ∂2v ∂x2 . (45) This is the heat conduction equation. To obtain a solution of this we again consider the velocity to be in the form of v = u0e i(kx−ωt) 28 and substituting this into the heat conduction equation (45) we obtain −iωu0e i(kx−ωt) = −k2νu0e i(kx−ωt) or iω = k2ν. Solving for k gives us k = √ iω ν = ±(1 + i) √ ω 2ν . In this case, we only consider the positive solution due to the requirement of the velocity needing to decrease as you move into the ﬂuid, so the solution of our velocity is v = u0e −x/δe i(x/δ−ωt) where δ = √ 2ν ω which deﬁnes the depth of penetration for a wave in this system. We can see from this solution that transverse waves occur in viscous ﬂuids however they are damped exponentially as we move away from the surface. We also see from δ with increasing frequency comes decreasing depth of penetration. The depth of penetration also increases with increasing kinematic viscosity. 4.2 The Damping Coefﬁcient In our previous section on gravity waves we had arrived at equations which represent the path of a ﬂuid particle and velocity wave of propagation, however, we never consid- ered the effect of damping on the wave propagation. The factor that will discuss in this section we shall denote as the pressure effect. The pressure effect arises when a change in the wind speed passing over a surface ﬂuctuates. This ﬂuctuation in wind speed will result in the air pressure above the surface changing over time. During our analysis of capillary waves, we found a formula to relate the difference in pressure in two media to the radii of curvature this formula is given by p − p0 = −α( ∂2ζ ∂x2 + ∂2ζ ∂y2 ) , where here p0 is given by the constant internal pressure and p is given by the pressure at the surface. We can extend this further by expressing a value for the pressure at the surface. To do this we must consider a form of Bernoulli’s equation, p = c − ρ 2 v2 − gρz. From this, it is easy to observe that the pressure will decrease at velocity increases. From this observation, it follows that for ﬂows of wind that have a relatively high ve- locity we will ﬁnd a greater difference between the pressure in the atmosphere and the internal pressure. This implies that when the wind blows over the surface the radii of curvature is dependant on the velocity of the wind. More speciﬁcally the larger the ve- 48 locity of the wave the larger the radii of curvature for the surface. Another important feature of these wind-generated waves is that the shape of the cap- illary waves ampliﬁes the pressure difference between the two adjoining media. This ampliﬁcation is due to the velocity of the wind increasing at the surface as the wind passes over the crest of a capillary wave, hence creating a lowering the pressure further at this point. Similarly, the velocity of the wind passing of the surface at the trough will decrease hence resulting in a larger pressure at this point. The reason for this change in velocity is due to the fact that as the wind approaches a crest of a wave the wind will ﬁnd a blockage in its natural horizontal ﬂow forcing the air to travel over the wave, at the top of the wave there will be horizontal ﬂow along the surface of the same velocity which will combine with the air attempting to pass over the wave which results in a higher overall velocity at the crest.
